item.title: OSSTagLab: decoding the sound of golf club tags
item.description:
Shot tracking tags sit on each club and tell a phone which club is out and when it is hit. They do it with sound. Each tag sends short tones between 17 and 20 kHz, above what most adults can hear and inside what a laptop or phone microphone can record.

We want club tagging to be open to anybody. So we recorded a set of 12 tags with a MacBook microphone, worked out what they send, and documented it here. OSSTagLab is the web app we built to do it. It shows the signal live, decodes it, and names the club. It is open source.

How we listened

We studied the tones as pictures.

Record. The browser records the microphone at 48 kHz, which is 48,000 samples per second. A recording holds frequencies up to half its sample rate, the Nyquist frequency, so 48 kHz covers everything up to 24 kHz. The app asks the browser to switch off echo cancellation, noise suppression, automatic gain and voice isolation, so the microphone signal arrives as recorded.

Draw a spectrogram. A spectrogram is a picture of sound with time across, frequency up, and brightness for loudness. It is made with a short-time Fourier transform. The recording is cut into short overlapping slices, and a fast Fourier transform on each slice shows which frequencies are in it. Each slice is faded in and out with a Hann window, which reduces spectral leakage and keeps each peak narrow.

Follow the tone. Each slice has one strong peak, the tone the tag is sending. The decoder uses slices 10 ms long, one every millisecond. It pads each slice with zeros to 2,048 points for a finer frequency grid, then fits a curve through the peak. That places the tone to within about 10 Hz. It keeps the strongest frequency between 16.5 and 21 kHz when that peak is 15 dB above the noise around it. The result is one frequency per millisecond.

Read the steps. Every signal a tag sends is a pattern of steps, small jumps in frequency, in that track. Sending data by switching between tones is called frequency-shift keying. With eight tones to choose from it is multiple frequency-shift keying.

For close study the app also cuts a recording down to a band around the tag tones with a band-pass filter and plots its level and its instantaneous frequency over time.

What we found

Each tag has a rest tone near 18 kHz, the tone it holds between signals. A signal is a pattern of short steps away from that tone and back. A tag makes one tone at a time.

A tag has two triggers. Light wakes it, and a hit changes what it sends. That gives three signals:

Signal When What it is What it tells the phone
Wake tone The tag wakes One steady tone for about 0.4 s A club is out
Resting frame While the tag is awake Six 10 ms tones around the rest tone, repeated every 172 ms Which club
After hit signal After a hit The rest tone moves up 1 kHz and hops at a fixed interval The club was hit

A 9 iron sends all three in four seconds.

The sections below take each signal in turn, then the putter, which differs in two ways.

The wake tone

A tag wakes when light reaches it. We woke ours with a flashlight. On the course the same thing happens when the club comes out of the bag.

The tag starts with one steady tone that lasts about 0.4 seconds. On our 11 clubs from driver to wedge the wake tone sits about 0.9 kHz above the rest tone, between 18.68 and 18.92 kHz.

The rest tone and the resting frame

About half a second after the wake tone ends, the tag settles on its rest tone. Our tags rest between 17.78 and 18.02 kHz.

Every 172 ms the tag sends a frame. A frame is six symbols. Each symbol is a 10 ms tone, and a new symbol starts about every 20 ms. Between symbols the tag returns to its rest tone.

A symbol is a step away from the rest tone. Steps are 100 Hz each, and a symbol moves 1 to 4 steps up or down. We saw eight values per symbol. That is up to 3 bits per symbol and 18 bits per frame.

One frame from the 9 iron, up close:

This frame reads +4 −1 −2 +1 −4 −3. Every club in the bag has a different frame, so the frame names the club.

The tag repeats its resting frame while it stays in the light. Our recordings show it repeating for about 6 seconds in a row. A phone that starts listening late still hears the club within a fraction of a second. When the light goes away the tag goes quiet.

The after hit signal

When the club is hit, the tag answers within about 12 ms. It moves its rest tone up by 1 kHz and starts a hop pattern. A hop is one jump up that lasts about 21 ms, then a return to the raised tone. The hops repeat at a fixed interval for several seconds. In our recordings the pattern ran for about 6.5 seconds after the last hit, then the resting frame came back.

Two numbers describe a hop pattern: the size of the jump and the time between jumps. Our tags jump 200, 300, 400 or 500 Hz, and they jump every 60, 80, 100 or 120 ms. Those intervals are 3, 4, 5 and 6 symbol slots of about 20 ms.

The figure shows measured values. The text rounds them.

The hop pattern reports the hit. Two pairs of clubs share a pattern. The 7 iron and 9 iron both jump 400 Hz every 60 ms, and the 56° wedge and approach wedge both jump 300 Hz every 120 ms. The resting frame heard just before the hit says which club it was.

How the putter is different

The putter tag follows the same plan with two changes.

Its wake tone is 19.81 kHz. That is 1.9 kHz above its rest tone and about 1 kHz above every other club’s wake tone.

After a hit it stays on its rest tone and sends a second frame. Its resting frame is −4 −2 −1 −3 −1 +1. Its frame after a hit is +1 +3 +4 +2 +4 −1. All six symbols change. The second frame starts about 60 ms after the tap and repeats for about two seconds. Then the resting frame comes back.

The app’s analysis view shows the full putter sequence, with each signal labeled.

The top panel is the spectrogram. The middle panel is the level in the tag band. The bottom panel is the frequency of the signal over time, where each symbol shows as a step.

All 12 clubs

Frequencies are in kHz. Each frame is six symbols in steps of 100 Hz from the rest tone.

Club Rest tone Resting frame Wake tone After a hit
Driver 17.86 −2 +3 −2 −3 −4 −3 18.76 +400 Hz every 100 ms
9 Wood 17.90 −1 +2 +3 +2 +4 −3 18.79 +200 Hz every 60 ms
4 Iron 17.97 +1 +2 +3 −4 −4 −3 18.86 +500 Hz every 120 ms
6 Iron 17.93 −3 +2 +2 +2 +3 −3 18.82 +500 Hz every 80 ms
7 Iron 17.78 −4 −2 +2 +3 −4 −3 18.68 +400 Hz every 60 ms
8 Iron 17.88 +3 +4 −2 +3 +4 −3 18.76 +400 Hz every 120 ms
9 Iron 17.91 +4 −1 −2 +1 −4 −3 18.80 +400 Hz every 60 ms
Approach Wedge 18.02 −2 +2 −4 +3 +4 −3 18.92 +300 Hz every 120 ms
52° Wedge 17.94 +4 −4 −3 −4 +4 −3 18.83 +200 Hz every 120 ms
56° Wedge 17.83 +1 +3 +4 −3 +4 −3 18.72 +300 Hz every 120 ms
60° Wedge 17.92 +3 −1 +3 −2 +3 −3 18.82 +500 Hz every 60 ms
Putter 17.92 −4 −2 −1 −3 −1 +1 19.81 Frame +1 +3 +4 +2 +4 −1

Every resting frame from driver to wedge ends in −3. The putter’s ends in +1.

The hop values are rounded to the nearest 100 Hz and 20 ms. The measured values are in the repo.

Hearing the hit

The strike itself is also in the recording. It is a short click that covers every frequency, which is why it shows as a vertical line in the putter picture above. The decoder listens for it from 2 to 8 kHz, well below the tag band. In our test recordings the click is 28 to 36 dB louder than the room and lasts about 10 to 120 ms.

OSSTagLab counts a hit each time the tag answers. The click gives the time of the hit. A soft hit with a faint click still counts, because the tag’s answer is enough.

OSSTagLab

OSSTagLab runs on your own computer and listens through the browser.

What it does:

  • Live spectrogram. See the tag band as you shine a light on a tag.
  • Decoder. Reads the wake tone, the resting frame and the after hit signal from the microphone.
  • Club mapping. Pick a club, light its tag, tap the club, and the app saves what it sends.
  • Identify. Light any mapped tag and the app names the club and counts each hit.
  • Captures. Save a few seconds of audio and study it in the analysis view.

It runs on Python 3.9 or newer and a browser. The server uses the Python standard library.

git clone https://github.com/OSSGolf/osstaglab
cd osstaglab
python3 server.py

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8765 and press Start listening.

OSSTagLab is an independent project, built by listening to our own set of tags. The decoder is plain JavaScript with tests and a set of short recordings, so anybody can port it to a phone or a microcontroller.

  • osstaglab (web app, decoder, recordings)

item.author: OSSGolf

item.title: Open source golf is exploding
item.description:
People are building launch monitors, shot trackers, course databases, and simulator engines in the open, and the list keeps getting longer.

Here are the projects we are watching right now.

Tap the map to open it full size.

Hardware

Launch monitors

Radar based

  • OpenFlight: A DIY golf launch monitor built around the OPS243-A Doppler radar on a Raspberry Pi, reporting ball speed, club speed, smash factor and estimated carry, with an optional TI IWR6843 radar for launch angle.
    • openflight-enclosure: 3D-printable enclosure for an OpenFlight monitor, with separate STL parts for the shell, radar and camera fronts, screen bezel and feet, plus CAD source. Minimum print bed is 220 by 190 mm.
    • openflight-mobile-kmp: A companion app for the OpenFlight launch monitor on Android and iOS, built with Kotlin Multiplatform and native UIs. It shows live shots, sessions and club stats over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth LE.
    • openflight-mobile: An Expo (React Native) companion app for OpenFlight that connects to the server over a socket connection and mirrors the live shot data from the web UI.

Camera based

  • PiTrac: A launch monitor that uses low-cost Raspberry Pi computers and cameras to measure ball launch speed, angles and spin in three dimensions. It feeds GSPro and E6/TruGolf simulators and a standalone web app.
  • LaunchTrac: A DIY golf launch monitor in Rust for a Raspberry Pi 5, using two global shutter cameras and IR strobes to measure ball speed, launch angles and spin.

Hybrid

  • launch-monitor: A DIY golf launch monitor on a Raspberry Pi 5 that combines a camera for launch angle and spin, a 10.5 GHz Doppler radar with FFT for ball speed, and an IR trigger for timing.

On-course trackers

GPS

  • open-gps: A handheld golf shot tracker on an ESP32-S3 with a u-blox GPS module. It saves each shot’s start and landing coordinates and distance in yards, exportable over USB as GeoJSON or CSV.

Training aids

Tempo

  • OSSTempo: A golf tempo trainer built from an ESP32 and a WS2812B LED strip, where a light comet sweeps the strip to pace the stroke. A Web Bluetooth page controls it.
    • osstempo-ios: A native SwiftUI and CoreBluetooth iPhone app that connects to the OSSTempo ESP32 trainer over Bluetooth LE, selects modes, triggers strokes and tunes settings with a live preview.

Biomechanics

Force plates

  • open-fp: Open source golf force plates, one per foot, each with four 50 kg load cells read by an Arduino UNO Q. It reports vertical force, center of pressure and weight shift on a web dashboard. Still in hardware bring-up.

3D printable

Swing trainers

  • Golf Zwing Trainer V4: A 3D printable swing plane trainer for left and right handers. It holds printed alignment sticks at set angles to guide a shallower downswing, and the base can be weighted with lead or BBs.

Range accessories

  • Golf Ball Dispenser Pro: A fully 3D printed golf ball dispenser with no extra hardware. Its magazine holds 25 balls and a foot pedal places one ball on the tee per press. Sized to print on an A1 mini.

Software

Simulators

Engines

  • OpenShotGolf: A Godot-based golf simulator that takes shot data from the PiTrac launch monitor or GSPro-style interfaces and models ball flight with drag and Magnus lift.
  • Seneca-Golf: An open source golf simulator built on the Urho3D game engine, intended as a base for DIY launch monitor, course building and game design work.
  • GolfForge: An open source golf simulator built in Unreal Engine 5 that builds courses from LIDAR and OpenStreetMap data and accepts launch monitor input through GSPro Open Connect connectors.
  • FUSE: A lightweight 3D golf physics and simulation engine from OpenGolfSim for WebGL-capable browsers, built on Three.js and WebGPU. It is licensed under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0.
  • cyberflight: A Rust 3D driving range that displays shots received from flighthook, an open source golf automation bus, over a local WebSocket.
  • Open-Birdie: An Electron desktop golf simulator that plays OpenStreetMap courses with AWS terrain elevation data and accepts shots from GSPro Open Connect launch monitors such as the Uneekor EYEMINI LITE.
  • uopengolf: An open source golf game for Windows and Linux built in Unreal Engine 5 with C++, with a savanna driving range, a 400-yard par 4, and Square Home or Open Connect launch monitor support.

Ball flight physics

  • Simple-Golf-Simulator: A Python and Tkinter program that simulates a golf swing from a two-degree-of-freedom model, then computes launch speed and the ball’s flight with drag, lift, spin and wind.
  • openfairway: A Godot 4 physics addon, usable from C# and GDScript, that computes ball flight, bounce and surface interaction from aerodynamic drag and Magnus lift fits.
  • libgolf: A C++20 library that simulates a golf ball’s full flight from launch conditions: aerial arc, bounce, and roll. Aerodynamics, bounce, and roll models are pluggable, and it builds to WebAssembly.
  • dimple: A pure Rust crate, with no dependencies, that turns launch-monitor numbers into a full golf shot: flight, bounce, and roll on turf. Air density and wind are configurable.

Course building

  • TGC-Designer-Tools: Python tools for course creation and lidar terrain generation in The Golf Club 2019. The main entry points are a GUI, a lidar map API, and an image-based terrain tool.
  • course-terrain-tool: A desktop app that searches free lidar sources, merges and crops LAZ or DEM files, and outputs raw Unity height maps and satellite overlay images for golf simulator courses.
  • course-meshery-tool: A JavaScript course-building tool from OpenGolfSim that generates base course meshes from an SVG file and a raw height map.

Launch monitor connectivity

Protocol libraries

  • gsp-r10-adapter: A C# utility that bridges a Garmin Approach R10 launch monitor to GSPro, with direct Bluetooth, an E6 Connect compatible server, and webcam putting options.
  • 10over: A Rust client library for the Garmin R10 Bluetooth protocol that decodes BLE, GFDI, and protobuf messages into shot data through a poll-based API.
  • ironsight: A Rust client library for the FlightScope Mevo+, Mevo Gen2, and Xi radar launch monitors, speaking their binary protocol over TCP with a poll-based API.
  • allsquare: A Rust client library for the Square Golf Omni launch monitor’s BLE protocol, reporting ball and club metrics through a poll-based API, plus a Flight Relay launch monitor binary.
  • R10Kit: A pure Swift package that connects to a Garmin R10 launch monitor over Bluetooth Low Energy and exposes shot metrics, including practice swings without a ball, for iOS, watchOS and macOS apps.
  • Flight Relay Protocol: An open JSON message spec, released under CC0, for sending launch monitor shot data over a local WebSocket to simulators, stat trackers and other tools.

Bridges to simulators

  • MLM2PRO-GSPro-Connector: A Windows GUI application written in Python that sends Rapsodo MLM2PRO and Mevo+ shots to GSPro, with optional webcam or ExPutt putting support.
  • MLM2PRO-BT-APP: A beta Windows app in C# that connects a Rapsodo MLM2PRO to simulator software over direct Bluetooth through the Open API, with an optional API relay for other connectors.
  • GSPro-MLM2PRO-OCR: A Python app that reads Rapsodo MLM2PRO metrics from a mirrored phone or tablet screen using OpenCV and Tesseract OCR, then sends them to GSPro.
  • flighthook: A Rust bridge that decodes shots from launch monitors such as FlightScope, Square Golf Omni and Garmin R10, and forwards them to simulators like GSPro.
  • gspro-bridge: A C# Windows bridge, in early development, intended to send Garmin R10 and optional webcam putting shots to GSPro. The README says it is not yet ready for use.
  • fairway-bridge: A Go application that connects launch monitors, simulators and cameras over a network, with a web UI, shot data logging to CSV, and virtual shot emulation for testing.

Swing analysis

Video and pose

  • GolfPosePro: A Jupyter notebook for Google Colab that uses MediaPipe Pose to track wrist motion, split a swing into phases, and compare student and pro frames in annotated slow-motion videos.
  • GolfSwingAnalyzer: A Python PyQt5 app that estimates body joints in 3D from two synchronized videos of a swing, plotting the skeleton with OpenGL and exporting joint coordinates to CSV.
  • Pose2Par: A desktop UI and Docker pipeline that turns a standard swing video into biomechanical data using MMPose pose estimation, ML marker enhancement and OpenSim. It reports pelvis and torso rotation, X-factor and swing event timing.
  • golf-swing-analysis: A Python script that tracks ear, hip and wrist landmarks with MediaPipe Pose on a down-the-line swing video, draws the swing angle and an X/Y axis overlay, and saves an annotated MP4.
  • PinPoint Studio: A beta, cross-platform desktop app in C++ and Qt for swing analysis. It combines multi-camera video, IMU wrist sensors and launch monitors, runs pose estimation locally, and reports metrics for each shot.
    • PinPointCapture: The iPhone companion app for PinPoint Studio, which joins a session as a camera over WiFi or USB. This repository also holds its requirements, design mockups and protocol conformance records.

Wearable

  • iSwing: A watchOS and iOS app that records golf swings with Apple Watch motion sensors and reports swing speed, attack angle, tempo and a machine-learning quality rating.

Camera ball tracking

Putting

  • cam-putting-py: A webcam putting simulator for GSPro that tracks a colored ball to calculate putt speed in mph and horizontal launch angle. Shots go to a Garmin R10 or MLM2PRO connector, which passes them to GSPro.

Course data

Databases and APIs

  • golf-data-docs: Generated documentation for the Golf Data API, covering clubs, courses, markers and holes. The API currently holds only UK course data.
  • OpenGolfAPI: A community-maintained REST API for golf courses worldwide, with tee sets, hole-by-hole data, climate normals and nearby places. No key is needed for 1,000 requests a day per IP; a free key raises the limit.
    • mcp-server: An MCP server that lets AI assistants search golf courses, scorecards, tees and weather from OpenGolfAPI, with an optional free key for logging shots and running tournaments.
  • GeoJSON-GolfCourses: A GeoJSON file of named golf course boundaries in North America, extracted from OpenStreetMap ways tagged leisure=golf_course. European courses are listed as coming soon.

Stats and scoring

Launch monitor data

  • TrackPull: A Chrome extension that pulls shot data from Trackman reports and Trackman portal sessions, then exports it as CSV, copies it to Google Sheets, or builds a prompt for an AI chatbot.
  • r10progress: A TypeScript web app that imports CSV shot exports from the Garmin Approach R10 radar, stores them in Firebase, and charts shot trends with Vega and a sortable ag-Grid table.

Rounds and handicap

  • garmin_golf: Browser scripts that export your own Garmin Connect golf scorecards and CT10 shot data as JSON, since Garmin has no public API. Includes jq and Google Sheets processing.
  • ghin: An unofficial TypeScript library, installed from npm, that wraps the GHIN handicap API for handicap lookups, golfer and course search, scoring history and course handicap calculation.
  • golf-app: A Java Spring Boot back-end for online scorecards, round results including Stableford and score differential, tournaments, and player result comparison.
  • opengolfapp: A free, open source golf tracking app for web, iOS and Android, with a React web app and Expo mobile app that logs shots, computes strokes gained, shot dispersion and handicap index.

Tour data

  • data-golf-api: An unofficial Python client for the DataGolf API, installed from PyPI as data_golf, covering general, prediction, betting and historical endpoints. Requires a paid DataGolf API key.

We will keep adding to this list as more projects show up.

GPS

  • open-gps: A handheld golf shot tracker on an ESP32-S3 with a u-blox GPS module. It saves each shot’s start and landing coordinates and distance in yards, exportable over USB as GeoJSON or CSV.

Training aids

Tempo

  • OSSTempo: A golf tempo trainer built from an ESP32 and a WS2812B LED strip, where a light comet sweeps the strip to pace the stroke. A Web Bluetooth page controls it.
    • osstempo-ios: A native SwiftUI and CoreBluetooth iPhone app that connects to the OSSTempo ESP32 trainer over Bluetooth LE, selects modes, triggers strokes and tunes settings with a live preview.

Biomechanics

Force plates

  • open-fp: Open source golf force plates, one per foot, each with four 50 kg load cells read by an Arduino UNO Q. It reports vertical force, center of pressure and weight shift on a web dashboard. Still in hardware bring-up.

3D printable

Swing trainers

  • Golf Zwing Trainer V4: A 3D printable swing plane trainer for left and right handers. It holds printed alignment sticks at set angles to guide a shallower downswing, and the base can be weighted with lead or BBs.

Range accessories

  • Golf Ball Dispenser Pro: A fully 3D printed golf ball dispenser with no extra hardware. Its magazine holds 25 balls and a foot pedal places one ball on the tee per press. Sized to print on an A1 mini.

Software

Simulators

Engines

  • OpenShotGolf: A Godot-based golf simulator that takes shot data from the PiTrac launch monitor or GSPro-style interfaces and models ball flight with drag and Magnus lift.
  • Seneca-Golf: An open source golf simulator built on the Urho3D game engine, intended as a base for DIY launch monitor, course building and game design work.
  • GolfForge: An open source golf simulator built in Unreal Engine 5 that builds courses from LIDAR and OpenStreetMap data and accepts launch monitor input through GSPro Open Connect connectors.
  • FUSE: A lightweight 3D golf physics and simulation engine from OpenGolfSim for WebGL-capable browsers, built on Three.js and WebGPU. It is licensed under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0.
  • cyberflight: A Rust 3D driving range that displays shots received from flighthook, an open source golf automation bus, over a local WebSocket.
  • Open-Birdie: An Electron desktop golf simulator that plays OpenStreetMap courses with AWS terrain elevation data and accepts shots from GSPro Open Connect launch monitors such as the Uneekor EYEMINI LITE.
  • uopengolf: An open source golf game for Windows and Linux built in Unreal Engine 5 with C++, with a savanna driving range, a 400-yard par 4, and Square Home or Open Connect launch monitor support.

Ball flight physics

  • Simple-Golf-Simulator: A Python and Tkinter program that simulates a golf swing from a two-degree-of-freedom model, then computes launch speed and the ball’s flight with drag, lift, spin and wind.
  • openfairway: A Godot 4 physics addon, usable from C# and GDScript, that computes ball flight, bounce and surface interaction from aerodynamic drag and Magnus lift fits.
  • libgolf: A C++20 library that simulates a golf ball’s full flight from launch conditions: aerial arc, bounce, and roll. Aerodynamics, bounce, and roll models are pluggable, and it builds to WebAssembly.
  • dimple: A pure Rust crate, with no dependencies, that turns launch-monitor numbers into a full golf shot: flight, bounce, and roll on turf. Air density and wind are configurable.

Course building

  • TGC-Designer-Tools: Python tools for course creation and lidar terrain generation in The Golf Club 2019. The main entry points are a GUI, a lidar map API, and an image-based terrain tool.
  • course-terrain-tool: A desktop app that searches free lidar sources, merges and crops LAZ or DEM files, and outputs raw Unity height maps and satellite overlay images for golf simulator courses.
  • course-meshery-tool: A JavaScript course-building tool from OpenGolfSim that generates base course meshes from an SVG file and a raw height map.

Launch monitor connectivity

Protocol libraries

  • gsp-r10-adapter: A C# utility that bridges a Garmin Approach R10 launch monitor to GSPro, with direct Bluetooth, an E6 Connect compatible server, and webcam putting options.
  • 10over: A Rust client library for the Garmin R10 Bluetooth protocol that decodes BLE, GFDI, and protobuf messages into shot data through a poll-based API.
  • ironsight: A Rust client library for the FlightScope Mevo+, Mevo Gen2, and Xi radar launch monitors, speaking their binary protocol over TCP with a poll-based API.
  • allsquare: A Rust client library for the Square Golf Omni launch monitor’s BLE protocol, reporting ball and club metrics through a poll-based API, plus a Flight Relay launch monitor binary.
  • R10Kit: A pure Swift package that connects to a Garmin R10 launch monitor over Bluetooth Low Energy and exposes shot metrics, including practice swings without a ball, for iOS, watchOS and macOS apps.
  • Flight Relay Protocol: An open JSON message spec, released under CC0, for sending launch monitor shot data over a local WebSocket to simulators, stat trackers and other tools.

Bridges to simulators

  • MLM2PRO-GSPro-Connector: A Windows GUI application written in Python that sends Rapsodo MLM2PRO and Mevo+ shots to GSPro, with optional webcam or ExPutt putting support.
  • MLM2PRO-BT-APP: A beta Windows app in C# that connects a Rapsodo MLM2PRO to simulator software over direct Bluetooth through the Open API, with an optional API relay for other connectors.
  • GSPro-MLM2PRO-OCR: A Python app that reads Rapsodo MLM2PRO metrics from a mirrored phone or tablet screen using OpenCV and Tesseract OCR, then sends them to GSPro.
  • flighthook: A Rust bridge that decodes shots from launch monitors such as FlightScope, Square Golf Omni and Garmin R10, and forwards them to simulators like GSPro.
  • gspro-bridge: A C# Windows bridge, in early development, intended to send Garmin R10 and optional webcam putting shots to GSPro. The README says it is not yet ready for use.
  • fairway-bridge: A Go application that connects launch monitors, simulators and cameras over a network, with a web UI, shot data logging to CSV, and virtual shot emulation for testing.

Swing analysis

Video and pose

  • GolfPosePro: A Jupyter notebook for Google Colab that uses MediaPipe Pose to track wrist motion, split a swing into phases, and compare student and pro frames in annotated slow-motion videos.
  • GolfSwingAnalyzer: A Python PyQt5 app that estimates body joints in 3D from two synchronized videos of a swing, plotting the skeleton with OpenGL and exporting joint coordinates to CSV.
  • Pose2Par: A desktop UI and Docker pipeline that turns a standard swing video into biomechanical data using MMPose pose estimation, ML marker enhancement and OpenSim. It reports pelvis and torso rotation, X-factor and swing event timing.
  • golf-swing-analysis: A Python script that tracks ear, hip and wrist landmarks with MediaPipe Pose on a down-the-line swing video, draws the swing angle and an X/Y axis overlay, and saves an annotated MP4.
  • PinPoint Studio: A beta, cross-platform desktop app in C++ and Qt for swing analysis. It combines multi-camera video, IMU wrist sensors and launch monitors, runs pose estimation locally, and reports metrics for each shot.
    • PinPointCapture: The iPhone companion app for PinPoint Studio, which joins a session as a camera over WiFi or USB. This repository also holds its requirements, design mockups and protocol conformance records.

Wearable

  • iSwing: A watchOS and iOS app that records golf swings with Apple Watch motion sensors and reports swing speed, attack angle, tempo and a machine-learning quality rating.

Camera ball tracking

Putting

  • cam-putting-py: A webcam putting simulator for GSPro that tracks a colored ball to calculate putt speed in mph and horizontal launch angle. Shots go to a Garmin R10 or MLM2PRO connector, which passes them to GSPro.

Course data

Databases and APIs

  • golf-data-docs: Generated documentation for the Golf Data API, covering clubs, courses, markers and holes. The API currently holds only UK course data.
  • OpenGolfAPI: A community-maintained REST API for golf courses worldwide, with tee sets, hole-by-hole data, climate normals and nearby places. No key is needed for 1,000 requests a day per IP; a free key raises the limit.
    • mcp-server: An MCP server that lets AI assistants search golf courses, scorecards, tees and weather from OpenGolfAPI, with an optional free key for logging shots and running tournaments.
  • GeoJSON-GolfCourses: A GeoJSON file of named golf course boundaries in North America, extracted from OpenStreetMap ways tagged leisure=golf_course. European courses are listed as coming soon.

Stats and scoring

Launch monitor data

  • TrackPull: A Chrome extension that pulls shot data from Trackman reports and Trackman portal sessions, then exports it as CSV, copies it to Google Sheets, or builds a prompt for an AI chatbot.
  • r10progress: A TypeScript web app that imports CSV shot exports from the Garmin Approach R10 radar, stores them in Firebase, and charts shot trends with Vega and a sortable ag-Grid table.

Rounds and handicap

  • garmin_golf: Browser scripts that export your own Garmin Connect golf scorecards and CT10 shot data as JSON, since Garmin has no public API. Includes jq and Google Sheets processing.
  • ghin: An unofficial TypeScript library, installed from npm, that wraps the GHIN handicap API for handicap lookups, golfer and course search, scoring history and course handicap calculation.
  • golf-app: A Java Spring Boot back-end for online scorecards, round results including Stableford and score differential, tournaments, and player result comparison.
  • opengolfapp: A free, open source golf tracking app for web, iOS and Android, with a React web app and Expo mobile app that logs shots, computes strokes gained, shot dispersion and handicap index.

Tour data

  • data-golf-api: An unofficial Python client for the DataGolf API, installed from PyPI as data_golf, covering general, prediction, betting and historical endpoints. Requires a paid DataGolf API key.

We will keep adding to this list as more projects show up.

item.title: Introducing OSSGolf
item.description:
Have you ever seen an overpriced golf gadget and thought “I could build that”?

You probably could. That is the whole idea behind OSSGolf.

Golf has a proud DIY history. Long before the big brands, players forged their own irons, turned persimmon heads by hand, and tweaked shafts in the garage until something worked. Tinkering helped build this game. Somewhere along the way, we handed all of it over to a checkout page.

Other hobbies never let that spirit die. People design and build experimental aircraft in their garages and actually fly them. Ham radio operators still solder their own rigs. There is no reason golf training should be any different.

OSSGolf brings it back. Open, free hardware and software for real training aids, documented well enough that you can build them yourself. A tempo trainer that costs tens of dollars in parts instead of the hundred plus you would pay off the shelf. A launch monitor SDK that lets your phone read a device you already own, with no subscription and no extra hardware.

The point is that you build it, you own it, you understand it, and you can change it.

Good training should not be locked behind a premium price tag. If you have ever wanted to build your own, this is the place.

Everything is open on GitHub: github.com/OSSGolf.

item.title: OSSTempo: a DIY LED tempo trainer for golf
item.description:
OSSTempo is an open source golf tempo trainer. A WS2812B LED strip animates a moving “comet” of light that sweeps along a channel, and you match your putter or club head to the dot to groove a consistent stroke.

It is a TempoStik style trainer built entirely from open hardware and firmware. An ESP32 drives a 144 LED per meter strip over a single data pin. Control happens over Bluetooth Low Energy, so a web page or the companion iOS app can set the tempo and stroke length.

Here it is running a putting stroke:

Two modes

  • Putting (2:1). The comet sweeps from center out to the top of the backswing, eases to a stop, then accelerates back through center at impact and out the far side on the follow through.
  • Full swing. The firmware models a full swing arc projected onto the one dimensional strip, so a one meter strip can represent a stroke that travels back and up behind you. Reference dots mark the ball, the top of the backswing, and an optional aim point.

Build it two ways

Same firmware, same app, two hardware paths:

  • Full DIY. A bare ESP32 dev board, a strip, one resistor, and one capacitor on a breadboard. Lowest cost.
  • QuinLED Dig2go. A pre assembled controller.

Both are documented end to end: bill of materials, wiring, flashing, and a pinned, ready to flash sketch.

Print a case and a jig

The repo now has two 3D printed parts. Each comes with STL files and a Bambu Studio project for the A1 mini.

Case. A snap shut case for the carrier PCB, an optional board the ESP32 plugs into. The board sits on four pegs through its mounting holes and the lid clips on by hand, with openings for the USB and strip cables. The golf ball badge and the oss/golf nameplate are separate parts that press into the lid, so they can be printed in a second color.

Alignment jig. A flat plate that holds two sticks parallel, 8 inches apart, with alignment lines grooved along it.

What is here today

The firmware, the Web Bluetooth control page, and a native SwiftUI iOS controller are all open source and working on real hardware. The build guides cover both hardware paths.

The clip above shows a putting stroke on a practice mat. For the full hardware spec and code, see GitHub.

  • osstempo (firmware, web control, docs)
  • osstempo-ios (native iOS controller)

item.title: R10Kit: an unofficial Swift SDK for the Garmin R10
item.description:
R10Kit is a native Swift SDK that connects directly to the Garmin Approach R10 launch monitor over Bluetooth Low Energy. No first party app, no PC tether. Your iPhone talks to the R10 and reads every shot it emits.

This is an unofficial SDK. The protocol layer is reverse engineered from publicly available work (mholow/gsp-r10-adapter).

The practice swing unlock

The interesting part is what the R10 gives you without a ball. On a full practice swing with no ball, the radar still reports club speed, club path, attack angle, and the full swing timing in milliseconds. R10Kit exposes all of it. That means you can build a tempo trainer around a launch monitor you already own, not just a ball flight tracer.

Ball metrics (ball speed, launch angle and direction, spin rate, spin axis) populate only when the radar sees a ball leave. Everything else populates on every swing.

Screenshots

The repo ships a runnable demo app. It shows connection state, device info, and a live list of recent shots. Tap a shot to see every field the SDK exposes.

What it parses

R10Kit does full proto parsing for every shot the device emits: club speed, ball speed, launch angle and direction, spin rate with axis and provenance, attack angle, club face and path, swing timing in milliseconds, shot type, and tilt at impact. The API is AsyncStream first, modern Swift Concurrency, no delegates.

  • iOS 17+, watchOS 10+, macOS 14+. Pure Swift package.
  • 70 unit tests covering framing, COBS, CRC, proto parsing, time base conversion, and the swing rejection detector.
  • Real byte regression fixtures captured from the device, so future changes cannot silently break protocol compatibility.

Tested against an R10 on firmware 4.50 with an iPhone 16 Pro.

Get it

  • unofficial-r10-ios-sdk on GitHub

Builds on mholow/gsp-r10-adapter, under the same MIT license.
